arguments.abstract: The selection of the appropriate machine learning algorithm for tabular prediction and classification tasks remains a weak point in many analytics pipelines in Indonesia. Practitioners often choose algorithms based on trends rather than actual data profiles and computational costs. This study evaluates three algorithms — Random Forest, XGBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron — on four public datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository: Adult Income (48,842 instances), Wine Quality (6,497 instances), Heart Disease (1,025 instances), and Pima Indians Diabetes (768 instances). Experiments employed 10-fold cross-validation, an 80/20 train–test split, and grid-based hyperparameter search. XGBoost achieved the highest average accuracy of 92.7% and an F1-score of 0.918 across datasets, outperforming Random Forest (89.4%; F1 = 0.881) and Neural Network (90.6%; F1 = 0.894). Interestingly, Neural Network excelled on the Wine Quality dataset whose features are mostly continuous, while XGBoost dominated on heterogeneous data with many categorical features. XGBoost training time (12.3 seconds) was substantially shorter than Neural Network (156.7 seconds) on identical hardware. These findings provide practical guidance for researchers and practitioners at Indonesian institutions: algorithm selection should be based on data characteristics and computational budget, not the popular assumption that deep learning is always superior for tabular problems.

arguments.rewrite:
This comparative study evaluated Random Forest, XGBoost, and MLP Neural Network on four public UCI datasets (total 57,132 instances) with a uniform preprocessing pipeline and validation protocol. XGBoost recorded the highest average accuracy (92.7%) and F1-score of 0.918, outperforming Random Forest (89.4%; F1 = 0.881) and MLP (90.6%; F1 = 0.894). However, the winner is not uniform — MLP narrowly excelled on Wine Quality (91.2%) whose features are purely continuous, while XGBoost dominated heterogeneous data with categorical features. On computational cost, XGBoost also excelled: 12.3 seconds training time for Adult Income versus 156.7 seconds for MLP. The conclusion: for small- to medium-scale tabular classification problems, XGBoost remains a reasonable default choice — unless the dataset features are purely numerical and of sufficient size, in which case MLP deserves consideration.

Several limitations must be honestly acknowledged. First, we only tested four datasets; generalization to multimodal or time-series datasets requires separate study. Second, the MLP we used is relatively simple (3 hidden layers); more modern tabular architectures such as TabNet or FT-Transformer may close the gap. Third, hyperparameters were tuned via limited grid search — Bayesian optimization may yield slightly higher results for MLP. Fourth, we did not test robustness against concept drift or distribution shift, which are important in real-world deployment.

Future research should pursue three concrete directions. (1) Expanding the benchmark to 15–20 datasets with more diverse profiles, including proprietary datasets from the Indonesian context (BPS data, Ministry of Health data) for local domain validation. (2) Adding modern baselines such as TabNet, CatBoost, and FT-Transformer so that the deep learning comparison is more complete; the claim that "MLP loses" cannot be overturned without testing contemporary tabular architectures. (3) Including structured explainability analysis using SHAP or LIME — because in many Indonesian contexts (banking, healthcare), interpretability is as important as accuracy, and this trade-off remains insufficiently documented in the local literature. The open question: at what point is an additional 1–2 points of accuracy worth a 10× computational cost? That is a question that must be answered per case, not in general.

arguments.text: Random Forest sudah lama menjadi pilihan default untuk klasifikasi tabular karena kemampuannya menangani fitur campuran dan ketahanannya terhadap overfitting. Nugroho (2025) secara khusus menganalisis bagaimana RF mengatasi overfitting melalui mekanisme bagging dan random feature subsampling, mencatat penurunan variansi prediksi hingga 23% dibanding decision tree tunggal pada dataset prediksi yang dia uji. Tapi studinya berhenti di analisis algoritmik — tidak membandingkan RF dengan boosting modern. Wiratama dan Aziz (2024) menerapkan RF untuk prediksi stunting balita dan mendapat akurasi 84,2%, sedikit lebih tinggi dari SVM (82,1%); kelemahan studinya adalah jumlah sampel terbatas (912 instans) sehingga sulit menggeneralisasi. Firnanda et al. (2025) membandingkan Decision Tree dan Random Forest untuk klasifikasi penjualan supermarket — RF unggul jelas (91,2% vs 86,4% akurasi), tetapi mereka mengakui waktu pelatihan RF sekitar 4,7 kali lebih lama. Inayah dan Ramli (2024) menggunakan RF untuk Intrusion Detection System pada dataset honeynet BSSN; akurasi mencapai 96,8% setelah penanganan kelas tidak seimbang, namun mereka menyoroti bahwa performa turun ke 89,3% tanpa SMOTE. Wibowo dan Gunawan (2025) menggunakan RF untuk memprediksi attrition karyawan dengan F1 0,876, walaupun mereka tidak menguji robustness terhadap missing data. Pola yang konsisten: RF kuat sebagai baseline, tapi performanya dipengaruhi imbalance dan jumlah fitur.
arguments.rewrite: Random Forest has long been the default choice for tabular classification due to its ability to handle mixed features and its robustness against overfitting. Nugroho (2025) specifically analyzed how RF overcomes overfitting through bagging mechanisms and random feature subsampling, noting a prediction variance reduction of up to 23% compared to a single decision tree on the prediction dataset he tested. However, his study stops at algorithmic analysis — it does not compare RF with modern boosting. Wiratama and Aziz (2024) applied RF for predicting childhood stunting and achieved 84.2% accuracy, slightly higher than SVM (82.1%); the weakness of their study is the limited sample size (912 instances), making generalization difficult. Firnanda et al. (2025) compared Decision Tree and Random Forest for supermarket sales classification — RF clearly excelled (91.2% vs 86.4% accuracy), but they acknowledged that RF training time was approximately 4.7 times longer. Inayah and Ramli (2024) used RF for an Intrusion Detection System on the BSSN honeynet dataset; accuracy reached 96.8% after handling class imbalance, yet they highlighted that performance dropped to 89.3% without SMOTE. Wibowo and Gunawan (2025) used RF to predict employee attrition with an F1 of 0.876, although they did not test robustness against missing data. A consistent pattern emerges: RF is strong as a baseline, but its performance is influenced by imbalance and the number of features.

arguments.text: XGBoost telah menjadi pemenang berulang di kompetisi Kaggle sejak 2016. Studi-studi di Indonesia ikut mengonfirmasi kekuatannya. Ais dan Sanjaya (2025) membandingkan RF, XGBoost, dan Logistic Regression untuk prediksi kekambuhan kanker tiroid; XGBoost mencapai akurasi 95,1% dibanding RF 92,4%, dan mereka menjelaskan keunggulan ini berasal dari kemampuan XGBoost mempelajari pola sekuensial pada residu. Tapi mereka tidak menguji Neural Network sebagai pembanding. Averina et al. (2025) memprediksi akun bot di media sosial X dengan tiga algoritma — XGBoost unggul (F1 = 0,927), namun pengujian dilakukan pada satu dataset proprietary saja. Andriansyah dan Fridayanthie (2023) menggabungkan SVM dan XGBoost dengan feature selection untuk klasifikasi kanker payudara; akurasi mencapai 97,8% setelah optimasi, dengan kelemahan utama: pipeline mereka membutuhkan tuning manual yang panjang. Rizaldi et al. (2025) menggunakan SVM dan XGBoost untuk analisis sentimen aplikasi Uber, dengan XGBoost mencapai akurasi 88,4% — namun precision turun signifikan (ke 0,79) pada kelas minoritas. Putra (2024) mengusulkan hibridisasi RF-XGBoost (RFXGB) untuk prediksi drop-out MOOC, melaporkan F1 0,894 — tapi metode hibrida ini menambah kompleksitas pipeline tanpa kenaikan akurasi yang besar dibanding XGBoost murni. Nabila dan Pamungkas (2025) membandingkan SVM, RF, dan XGBoost untuk prediksi stroke, dengan XGBoost paling unggul (akurasi 94,3%) tapi tanpa menyertakan baseline neural.
arguments.rewrite: XGBoost has been a repeated winner in Kaggle competitions since 2016. Studies in Indonesia have also confirmed its strength. Ais and Sanjaya (2025) compared RF, XGBoost, and Logistic Regression for predicting thyroid cancer recurrence; XGBoost achieved 95.1% accuracy compared to RF's 92.4%, and they explained this superiority stems from XGBoost's ability to learn sequential patterns in residuals. However, they did not test Neural Network as a comparator. Averina et al. (2025) predicted bot accounts on social media platform X using three algorithms — XGBoost excelled (F1 = 0.927), yet testing was conducted on only one proprietary dataset. Andriansyah and Fridayanthie (2023) combined SVM and XGBoost with feature selection for breast cancer classification; accuracy reached 97.8% after optimization, with the main weakness: their pipeline required lengthy manual tuning. Rizaldi et al. (2025) used SVM and XGBoost for sentiment analysis of the Uber app, with XGBoost achieving 88.4% accuracy — however, precision dropped significantly (to 0.79) on the minority class. Putra (2024) proposed RF-XGBoost hybridization (RFXGB) for MOOC drop-out prediction, reporting an F1 of 0.894 — but this hybrid method added pipeline complexity without a substantial accuracy increase over pure XGBoost. Nabila and Pamungkas (2025) compared SVM, RF, and XGBoost for stroke prediction, with XGBoost being the most superior (94.3% accuracy) but without including a neural baseline.

arguments.rewrite: Neural Networks — particularly Multi-Layer Perceptrons — are often assumed to be superior due to their representational capacity. However, on tabular data, their position is more ambiguous. Nurrokhman (2023) compared SVM and MLP for liver disease classification; MLP achieved 87.4% accuracy, only 1.1 points above SVM (86.3%), a difference that does not justify the additional computational cost. Pratama and Lestari (2024) tested MLP for predicting student academic performance with 3 hidden layers (128-64-32); accuracy reached 89.6%, but gradient vanishing became a problem when they deepened to 5 layers. The same study noted that MLP required careful feature scaling — without StandardScaler, accuracy fell to 74.2%, a finding consistent with standard MLP theory. Hidayat et al. (2025) compared CNN and MLP for ECG signal classification; CNN excelled because the data had structured temporal patterns. Their key insight: Neural Networks shine when a "natural" structure exists in the data — image, text, signal — but are often inferior to tree ensembles on tabular data without that structure.

arguments.rewrite: Each algorithm was run 10 times per dataset with stratified 10-fold cross-validation. We chose stratified because the class distribution is imbalanced in Adult Income and Pima — ordinary random k-fold is prone to producing folds with class ratios that deviate from the population. The classification threshold was set at 0.5 for all algorithms, without additional probability calibration. Metrics were calculated on the holdout test set that was never seen during tuning. As a sanity check, we also ran a majority-class baseline classifier on each dataset; this baseline failed to provide an F1 above 0.52, meaning all algorithms we tested truly learned meaningful patterns — not merely guessing the majority class.

arguments.rewrite: On average accuracy across four datasets, XGBoost recorded 92.7% — 3.3 points above Random Forest (89.4%) and 2.1 points above Neural Network (90.6%). This margin is consistent with the findings of Pourmoradian et al. (2026) on honey authentication, although our datasets differ greatly in domain. However, this headline number conceals far more interesting variation. On Wine Quality, MLP actually excelled (91.2% accuracy) over XGBoost (90.4%) and RF (87.9%). Why? Wine Quality features are purely continuous numerical — the type of data that advantages parametric models with smooth boundaries such as MLP. On Adult Income, the gap becomes reversed and sharp: XGBoost 87.3%, RF 85.1%, MLP only 82.4%. The cause: Adult Income has many categorical features (occupation, marital_status, education) that after one-hot encoding explode into hundreds of sparse dimensions — a condition that hinders MLP because default dropout and regularization are insufficient to handle extreme sparsity. XGBoost handles categorical features via tree splits that are inherently more efficient on one-hot data. Random Forest falls in the middle because its ensemble lacks a regularization mechanism as good as boosting. This observation is not new — but it is rarely displayed explicitly in Indonesian-language comparative papers.
